extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (readers of Kant)
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of Immanuel Kant's Critique of Judgment (aesthetics and teleology), extracting its descriptive and normative claims about judgments (aesthetic, teleological, moral) and reasoning methods. Useful for students, instructors, or scholars analyzing Kantian criteria for taste, teleology, analogy, and practical postulates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement of taste (disinterested satisfaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: "We view beautiful nature with favour, whilst we have a quite free (disinterested) satisfaction in its form. For in this mere judgement of taste no consideration is given to the purpose for which these natural beauties exist; whether to excite pleasure in us, or as purposes without any reference to us at all.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant distinguishes 'mere judgement of taste' from teleological judgement: when judging beauty properly one has a disinterested satisfaction focused on form, not on the object's purpose or utility. Avoid introducing considerations of purpose when making a pure aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleological judgement (attention to purposiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: "In a teleological judgement we pay attention to this reference, and here we can regard it as a favour of nature that it has been willing to minister to our culture by the exhibition of so many beautiful figures.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teleological judgements explicitly consider reference to purposes (e.g., nature's purposiveness) and may interpret natural beauty as serving human culture. Use teleological judgement when assessing purposive relations, but recognize it differs from disinterested aesthetic judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of the extent of our cognitive powers ('vermessen')
rubrics_metrics.description: "A judgement in which we forget to consider the extent of our powers (our Understanding) may sometimes sound very humble, and yet make great pretensions, and so be very presumptuous.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant warns against presumptuous judgements that overstep the limits of our understanding (vermessen). Critics should check whether they are ascribing to nature or the Divine more than human cognitive grounds permit; avoid treating speculative leaps as humble when they really assert more than warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical examination of judgement with respect to cognitive faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: "...abandon all these objective assertions and to examine critically our judgement merely in reference to our cognitive faculties, in order to supply to their principle a validity which, if not dogmatic, shall at least be that of a maxim sufficient for the sure employment of Reason.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In speculative matters one should suspend dogmatic objective claims and instead interrogate the faculties (how we judge) to formulate maxims that secure Reason's proper use. Preference for critical-reflective method over speculative assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and legitimate use of analogy in reasoning about purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: "Analogy (in a qualitative signification) is the identity of the relation between reasons and consequences... Thus we conceive of the artificial constructions of beasts by comparing them with those of men... But then I cannot therefore conclude that because man uses reason for his building, the beaver must have the like... I can conceive, according to the analogy of an Understanding, the causality of the supreme World-Cause, by comparing its purposive products in the world with the artificial works of men; but I cannot conclude according to analogy to those properties in it [which are in man]... the principle of the possibility of such a method of reasoning entirely fails, viz. the paritas rationis for counting the Supreme Being in one and the same genus with man.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy permits concluding similarity of relations (par ratio) but requires a parity of reasons (paritas rationis) to transfer properties; one may infer that nonhuman agents act by representations from similar effects, but may not infer human-like properties of a Supreme Being from analogy. Use analogy cautiously and check whether the necessary parity of reasons holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner moral worth: subordination under the principle of universal validity
rubrics_metrics.description: "This formal characteristic of my actions (their subordination under the principle of universal validity), wherein alone consists their inner moral worth, is quite in our power; and I can quite well abstract from the possibility or the unattainableness of purposes which I am obliged to promote in conformity with that law...",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral worth resides in acting from the form of the moral law (universalizability), not in success or external consequences. When evaluating moral action, assess whether it is performed from duty and conformity to a principle of universal validity rather than by reference to attainment of ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical postulates (God, immortality) as necessary for practical reason
rubrics_metrics.description: "...the speculative Reason fully convinces itself that the latter can never take place, but that on the other hand those Ideas whose object lies outside nature can be thought without contradiction, it must for its own practical law and the problem prescribed thereby, and therefore in a moral aspect, recognise those Ideas as real in order not to come into contradiction with itself.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant holds that speculative proof of God or immortality is not achieved, yet practical Reason must assume (postulate) such Ideas to coherently pursue moral ends. These are not objective proofs but necessary moral assumptions to avoid contradiction in practical deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of 'things of faith' as free belief compatible with morality
rubrics_metrics.description: "Things of faith are not therefore articles of faith; if we understand by the latter things of faith to the confession of which (internal or external) we can be bound. Natural theology contains nothing like this. For since they, as things of faith (like things of fact) cannot be based on theoretical proofs, [they are accepted by] a belief which is free and which only as such is compatible with the morality of the subject.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that cannot be grounded in theoretical proof may nevertheless be accepted as 'things of faith' through free belief; such acceptance must remain voluntary to remain compatible with moral agency. Do not conflate morally requisite assumptions with dogmatic confessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic admiration's capacity to evoke moral/religious feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: "The admiration for beauty, and also the emotion aroused by the manifold purposes of nature... have something in themselves like religious feeling. They seem in the first place by a method of judging analogous to moral to produce an effect upon the moral feeling (gratitude to, and veneration for, the unknown cause); and thus by exciting moral Ideas to produce an effect upon the mind...",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic judgment and teleological appreciation can trigger moral sentiments (gratitude, veneration) analogous to religious feeling. When evaluating aesthetic experience, consider its potential to influence moral sensibility, not merely theoretical cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Man as final purpose of creation (as moral, not merely happy, being)
rubrics_metrics.description: "...it is only as a moral being that man can be the final purpose of creation; but that as concerns his state happiness is only connected with it as a consequence, according to the measure of his harmony with that purpose regarded as the purpose of his being.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant distinguishes between happiness and moral finality: if there is an objective final purpose of creation it can only consist in man insofar as he is a moral being; happiness is at best a conditioned consequence. In judgments about teleology or cosmic purpose, prioritize moral purposiveness over mere happiness.
